name: Sprint/HIIT for growth hormone

lead: Some teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts because intense exercise triggers a growth hormone (GH) surge, and GH is the hormone most associated with childhood growth. The hope is that more GH signalling during puberty adds height.

Vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH pulses, and GH acts on growth cartilage directly and through IGF-1 from the liver. The exercise-GH link is documented, but reference sources do not state that exercise-triggered pulses change final adult height, and no published trial has tested sprint or HIIT training for adult height.

paras: People add sprint sessions or interval circuits to their weekly training during adolescence, often alongside sleep and nutrition habits they also link to growth. The workouts double as general conditioning and leanness work.

Sprint and interval training carry the usual risks of high-intensity exercise, such as muscle and tendon strain. Adult height is described as largely genetic, with nutrition and health as the main modifiable factors.

angle.text: Teens do sprints and HIIT because vigorous exercise briefly raises growth hormone, and they hope that extra signalling supports more growth. The short-term GH rise is documented; a link to final height has not been tested in trials.

lead: Sprint or high-intensity interval training (HIIT) for growth hormone is a height-related practice in which teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts in the belief that the resulting surge in growth hormone (GH) will help them grow taller or look more developed. It rests on the fact that vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH secretion, and GH is the hormone best known for its role in childhood growth.[1]

Wikipedia describes increased childhood height as GH's most widely known effect, working both directly on cartilage cells and through IGF-1 made mainly in the liver, and notes that young adolescents secrete roughly 700 micrograms a day versus about 400 in healthy adults.[1] HIIT itself is a training format that alternates short, intense anaerobic efforts with brief recoveries, and the same encyclopedia entry reports that in adolescents it can increase muscle mass, especially in the mid-to-late teens, and can reduce body fat in youth with obesity.[2] For appearance, that gives the practice a second payoff alongside the height hope: a leaner, more muscular build.

Adult height is described as largely heritable, with nutrition and health in childhood the main environmental factors.[3] No published trial has tested sprint or HIIT training as a way to change final height in healthy adolescents.
infobox: Short maximal sprints or interval circuits

paras: Practitioners describe short, maximal-effort sprints, hill sprints or interval circuits performed several times a week, sometimes combined with sleep and nutrition routines, with the stated aim of maximising natural GH release during the years when growth is still possible.
Wikipedia describes HIIT as alternating short intense bursts with brief recovery, with sessions typically under 30 minutes and a common ratio of about 2:1 work to rest.[2]

GH is released in pulses. Wikipedia lists sleep, vigorous exercise, fasting, sex hormones in puberty, ghrelin and others among stimulators, and describes the largest daily peak as occurring about an hour after sleep onset.[1] In children, GH deficiency causes growth failure and short stature, which underlies the idea that more GH could mean more height.[1]

Twin studies cited by Wikipedia estimate that 60 to 80 percent of height variation within a population is heritable, and growth reaches zero on average around 15 to 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males.[3] Chronic malnutrition during childhood is associated with reduced adult height.[3]

Wikipedia reports HIIT modestly reduces subcutaneous fat in healthy people and more in overweight people, and that in teens 8 to 12 weeks of HIIT combined with resistance training reduced waist size and body fat percentage in a 2021 review.[2] It also notes HIIT may be less effective than longer sessions for building muscle or bone mass.[2]
No studies found on sprint or HIIT training and final height in adolescents. Reference sources note that exercise raises GH levels temporarily.[1]

lore.intro: In height-focused forum discussion, sprinting and HIIT are often listed among free ways to support growth during puberty.
